news.title: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
news.title_en: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
news.author: Lily Hay Newman
news.article_content:
As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

This sandbox hosts realistic versions of social media, e-commerce, and banking platforms, allowing researchers to evaluate the resilience of Gemini-powered web-browsing agents against prompt-injection attacks and other real-world vulnerabilities without risking the open web.
paragraphs: As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step, there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

news.article_content:
Nov 19 (Reuters) - Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO brings to Wall Street an avatar of a sector that proponents herald as an economic panacea, while detractors warn it has stoked a market bubble and could ultimately threaten humanity itself.

More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker's debut after securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in the IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to the sector, even as a rocky market reception for Nvidia results which looked strong at first blush, signals the euphoria around the sector has cooled.

"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.

AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the incipient crushing debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.

An extramarital-affair scandal involving Nvidia's CEO and a spike in Treasury yields have further unnerved investors.

As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the roadshow. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion.

"Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.

paragraphs: Nov 19 (Reuters) - Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO brings to Wall Street an avatar of a sector that proponents herald as an economic panacea, while detractors warn it has stoked a market bubble and could ultimately threaten humanity itself.

More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker's debut after securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in the IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to the sector, even as a rocky market reception for Nvidia results which looked strong at first blush, signals the euphoria around the sector has cooled.

"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.
AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the incipient crushing debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.
An extramarital-affair scandal involving Nvidia's CEO and a spike in Treasury yields have further unnerved investors.
As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the roadshow. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion.

"Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive demand from index-tracking funds will account for about 28% of Anthropic's shares offered, or roughly $19 billion.
When it debuts on the Nasdaq later on Thursday, Anthropic will join the world's trillion-dollar club, alongside technology giants such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.
The listing will also give retail investors a chance to pile into one of the AI industry's hottest names, potentially amplifying swings in the stock as trading begins.
The buzz has already spilled onto prediction markets, where traders are placing bets on everything from its opening pop to where the stock will close on its first day.

Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, some of the world's biggest CEOs, and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.
Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.
"It doesn't have to be a bad company for it to be a bad investment at the IPO price," said Nic Puckrin, cross-asset analyst and founder of Coin Bureau.

Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control.

Investors will be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge as a proxy for the broader AI trade as questions over valuations, spending and returns weigh on sentiment.

The company will also need to balance growth with calls to slow the development of advanced AI models over concerns that they pose cybersecurity threats and could be exploited by bad actors to target critical government and private infrastructure.
Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that AI could behave unpredictably and advance faster than oversight mechanisms, posing potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

news.title: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
news.title_en: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
news.author: Emma Roth
news.article_content:
Anthropic has officially gone public. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT” at $111.50 per share, up from its initial $83 per share price that put company’s value at around $1.5 trillion.

The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans to go public. In its lengthy S-1 filing, the AI company reported recording an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year, most of which comes from an accounting charge that doesn’t reflect its business, along with $16.3 billion in revenue. The filing outlines plans that Anthropic says will help it develop AI for the benefit of humanity, which includes a governance structure that keeps control of the company in the hands of the founders, rather than the shareholders.

While speaking ahead of Anthropic’s debut at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei highlighted his stance on AI safety. “To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said, according to Reuters. “We will not bend to either business nor political pressure.”

Anthropic’s S-1 filing also listed possible “catastrophic” risks associated with its AI models, including “self-preserving behaviors” like resisting attempts to shut them down. It also warns potential shareholders that its AI models “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that can harm Anthropic.

Anthropic recently revealed that, like rival OpenAI, it has experienced incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environment and hacking third-party organizations. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a plan to slow down the training and development of AI in response to the wave of rogue AI cyberattacks. As part of that plan, it gave safety evaluators at METR “employee-like access” to its internal systems, who found that the company is using AI to accelerate its research and development.

A short seller's export-control allegations turned an early chip rally into a sharp reversal for Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD). AMD stock is trading at $487.80 as of 11:00 a.m. ET on Thursday, down 8% from Wednesday's close. The slide erased an early 3% gain that came as AMD shares rose with the rest of the chip group.

Hunterbrook says it's short AMD. The firm reported that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker the U.S. blacklisted in March 2025, kept posting Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) updates containing newer AMD firmware after the blacklisting. The firm said AMD didn't answer its questions and that its findings don't establish an export-law violation. AMD hadn't publicly responded to the report as of this writing.

The broader tech market is rebounding around the Nasdaq debut of Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), which makes AMD's reversal stand out. Anthropic is one of the lead customers running workloads on AMD's Helios rack-scale systems.

China's access to U.S. AI and server chips was already the market's hottest topic before Hunterbrook published its findings on November 19. President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. could allow sales of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) Blackwell chips to China in the future, Bloomberg reported. NVIDIA's guidance for Q4 FY2027 already assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China.

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

Any hint that AMD technology reached a blacklisted firm raises regulatory risk for a company now leaning heavily on server and AI demand. AMD's Data Center segment revenue rose 97% year over year (YoY) to $8.55 billion in Q3 2026. The company has previously cited government export regulations, tariffs and licensing requirements as risks. Executives on the company's November 3 earnings call didn't address China, export controls or restricted entities, leaving the market to consider Hunterbrook's claims without a direct response.

Despite the volatility of AMD stock, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock is still up 5% to $57.38. The company signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A chip process, news that's still lifting the shares. Intel's position as the rival x86 server processor maker adds context while Hunterbrook's allegations weigh on AMD.
NVIDIA stock is at $153.40, up 1.6%, so it's also holding steady despite the big swings of AMD stock today. Measured year to date (YTD), NVDA stock is down 18%.

AMD designs its chips and outsources manufacturing to third-party foundries and contract manufacturers, so its processors move through a wide network of server builders. Under this approach, AMD competes in server central processing units (CPUs) through EPYC and in AI accelerators through Instinct, which it packages together in Helios systems. Reliance on partners can also leave AMD with less direct control over where its technology ends up.

Intel takes the opposite approach, building chips in its own factories. Intel held its October 29 earnings call. On the call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated, "We are one of just three advanced-node semiconductor foundries in the world, and the only one domiciled in the United States." The U.S. government holds a significant equity interest in Intel.

NVIDIA, by contrast, is the dominant AI accelerator maker and competes most directly with AMD's Instinct line. Tan has targeted AMD in server processors too, saying Intel's next-generation product "will be ahead of AMD."

AMD's Q4 2026 revenue guidance of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3% offers bulls evidence that demand for its Instinct and EPYC chips remains strong. Speaking at the company's November 3 earnings release, CEO Lisa Su declared, "We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year." Hunterbrook's own statement that its findings don't establish an export-law violation gives AMD supporters another argument.

The bears counter that even unresolved questions about blacklisted buyers can invite scrutiny from regulators and customers, and AMD stock already carries high expectations after its run this year. The same AI data-center expansion driving EPYC and Instinct demand also runs through the power, cooling, and networking suppliers we profiled in a free report on seven AI infrastructure names that aren't chipmakers. AMD's next test is whether the company publicly addresses Hunterbrook's findings on IEIT Systems. A cautious approach could make sense for traders considering AMD stock until the export-compliance question around the company resolves.

news.author: Lisa Fickenscher
news.article_content:
Amazon customers in New York City will be charged up to $5 more per order if the local government passes a controversial bill aimed at cracking down on employment practices for “last-mile” delivery drivers, the e-tail giant is warning.

Amazon is appealing directly to its Big Apple customers in its fight against the legislation, The Post has learned.

Starting Thursday, they will see messages on Amazon’s website and app warning of higher costs if the bill passes.

Amazon is also urging customers to contact their City Council members, providing a form and link to send direct messages saying they don’t want “slower and more expensive” service.

“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written – which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement.

The appeal marks an escalation from Amazon’s efforts to date, which include months of TV ads about the bill’s potential impact.

The legislation aims to end Amazon’s reliance on subcontractors by requiring the e-commerce giant to get licenses for its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and hire delivery workers as full-timers. Other companies including FedEx would also be subject to the new rules.

The bill would affect over 5,000 delivery workers currently employed by about 40 third-party contractors, according to Amazon.

A supermajority of Council members — and far-left Mayor Zohran Mamdani — support the bill, which comes from Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens).

Proponents claim it would improve worker pay and safety by holding Amazon to a higher standard and making it liable for accidents involving its delivery operations.

Opponents say the legislation could cost thousands of jobs, with a group called New York Delivers threatening legal action earlier this week.

Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan) is in active negotiations with Amazon, the Teamsters union – which is advocating for the bill – and the city’s legal counsel, she told The Post last week.

“It’s time for Amazon to adhere to a licensing framework that ensures fair pay, strong worker protections, and more responsible delivery practices,” the lawmaker said.

Amazon has threatened to move its distribution centers outside the city to avoid the direct-hire mandate — saying it would have to fire some 2,000 warehouse workers who staff them — if the bill becomes law.

paragraphs: Amazon customers in New York City will be charged up to $5 more per order if the local government passes a controversial bill aimed at cracking down on employment practices for “last-mile” delivery drivers, the e-tail giant is warning.
Amazon is appealing directly to its Big Apple customers in its fight against the legislation, The Post has learned.
Starting Thursday, they will see messages on Amazon’s website and app warning of higher costs if the bill passes.
Amazon is also urging customers to contact their City Council members, providing a form and link to send direct messages saying they don’t want “slower and more expensive” service.

“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written – which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement.
The appeal marks an escalation from Amazon’s efforts to date, which include months of TV ads about the bill’s potential impact.

The legislation aims to end Amazon’s reliance on subcontractors by requiring the e-commerce giant to get licenses for its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and hire delivery workers as full-timers. Other companies including FedEx would also be subject to the new rules.
The bill would affect over 5,000 delivery workers currently employed by about 40 third-party contractors, according to Amazon.
A supermajority of Council members — and far-left Mayor Zohran Mamdani — support the bill, which comes from Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens).
Proponents claim it would improve worker pay and safety by holding Amazon to a higher standard and making it liable for accidents involving its delivery operations.
Opponents say the legislation could cost thousands of jobs, with a group called New York Delivers threatening legal action earlier this week.
Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan) is in active negotiations with Amazon, the Teamsters union – which is advocating for the bill – and the city’s legal counsel, she told The Post last week.
“It’s time for Amazon to adhere to a licensing framework that ensures fair pay, strong worker protections, and more responsible delivery practices,” the lawmaker said.

Amazon has threatened to move its distribution centers outside the city to avoid the direct-hire mandate — saying it would have to fire some 2,000 warehouse workers who staff them — if the bill becomes law.

“We’re hopeful that this bill doesn’t pass as written, but so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations and they haven’t taken us up on our offer to visit our sites and talk with the small businesses that work out of them every day,” Nantel said.
Some co-sponsors have begun to express concerns about the potential for job losses. Councilman Phil Wong (D-Queens) withdrew his support for the bill over that issue, as The Post previously reported.

news.title: Binance Secures $6.5 Billion Freezing Order From Abu Dhabi Court
news.title_en: Binance Secures $6.5 Billion Freezing Order From Abu Dhabi Court

inline_images.caption: Binance SAFU

news.author: Bloomberg
news.article_content:
Binance announced the court action on November 18, saying its legal representatives had identified approximately 26,000 cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with stolen assets. The exchange plans to maintain an updated list as investigators trace funds moving between wallets and blockchains.

The injunction follows an attack that Binance valued at approximately $6.34 billion. The company previously reported that about $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted, leaving substantial assets outside its immediate control.

The ADGM Courts granted a worldwide freezing injunction against unidentified defendants accused of carrying out the theft, alongside separate proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders intended to support asset recovery.

The $6.5 billion represents the amount covered by the legal order, not the value of cryptocurrency already secured. A freezing injunction restricts dealings with covered assets, while delivery-up orders provide a mechanism for requiring identified assets to be returned.

Some orders involve named parties that previously froze assets linked to the attack. Binance has not alleged wrongdoing by those parties, which include entities cooperating with recovery efforts.

The exchange said certain stablecoin issuers, cryptocurrency exchanges and other intermediaries require judicial authorization before transferring frozen assets to a claimant. The new orders are intended to provide that legal basis where applicable.

Gibson Dunn, the law firm representing Binance, said the orders can be served through blockchain transactions. Its lawyers also described the approximately 26,000 identified wallet addresses as a continuously updated list designed to help intermediaries recognize and restrict stolen funds.

However, identifying an address does not automatically establish that its current balance is recoverable. Effective enforcement depends on the relevant jurisdiction, the assets involved and whether an intermediary can prevent further transfers.

The $6.5 billion figure measures the injunction’s legal scope rather than Binance’s recovered assets. The financial benefit will depend on how much previously frozen cryptocurrency can actually be returned and whether additional stolen funds can be intercepted.

Binance’s earlier incident report placed the total value of affected cryptocurrency at approximately $6.34 billion, with around $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted as of November 3.

paragraphs: Binance announced the court action on November 18, saying its legal representatives had identified approximately 26,000 cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with stolen assets. The exchange plans to maintain an updated list as investigators trace funds moving between wallets and blockchains.

The injunction follows an attack that Binance valued at approximately $6.34 billion. The company previously reported that about $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted, leaving substantial assets outside its immediate control.

The ADGM Courts granted a worldwide freezing injunction against unidentified defendants accused of carrying out the theft, alongside separate proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders intended to support asset recovery.

The $6.5 billion represents the amount covered by the legal order, not the value of cryptocurrency already secured. A freezing injunction restricts dealings with covered assets, while delivery-up orders provide a mechanism for requiring identified assets to be returned.
Some orders involve named parties that previously froze assets linked to the attack. Binance has not alleged wrongdoing by those parties, which include entities cooperating with recovery efforts.

The exchange said certain stablecoin issuers, cryptocurrency exchanges and other intermediaries require judicial authorization before transferring frozen assets to a claimant. The new orders are intended to provide that legal basis where applicable.

Gibson Dunn, the law firm representing Binance, said the orders can be served through blockchain transactions. Its lawyers also described the approximately 26,000 identified wallet addresses as a continuously updated list designed to help intermediaries recognize and restrict stolen funds.

However, identifying an address does not automatically establish that its current balance is recoverable. Effective enforcement depends on the relevant jurisdiction, the assets involved and whether an intermediary can prevent further transfers.

The $6.5 billion figure measures the injunction’s legal scope rather than Binance’s recovered assets. The financial benefit will depend on how much previously frozen cryptocurrency can actually be returned and whether additional stolen funds can be intercepted.
Binance’s earlier incident report placed the total value of affected cryptocurrency at approximately $6.34 billion, with around $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted as of November 3.

The US Department of Justice subsequently announced on November 12 that coordinated government and private-sector efforts had frozen more than $2.7 billion, including more than $1.2 billion covered by US court authorization to seize or restrain assets.

Those figures should not be added together. The American enforcement actions concern assets within the broader pool of stolen cryptocurrency, and the announcements do not establish how much of the funds is independently covered by the different legal proceedings.

As FinanceFeeds previously examined, frozen assets are not equivalent to returned funds. Ownership, custody arrangements and judicial procedures can delay recovery even when issuers or exchanges have successfully restricted transfers.

The challenge is particularly pronounced for bitcoin and ether, which lack the centralized issuer controls available for freezing certain stablecoins. Funds held in self-custodied wallets generally cannot be immobilized merely by obtaining a court order.

Separately, Binance announced on November 12 that it had completed coverage of assets affected by the breach, using its corporate treasury, part of its Secure Asset Fund for Users and surplus futures insurance-fund resources.
The exchange also published a new proof-of-reserves snapshot covering 198 tokens. Replenishing customer-facing reserves is nevertheless distinct from recovering the original stolen cryptocurrency.

Successful asset recovery could eventually offset part of the resources Binance deployed to cover the breach. But the exchange does not publish comprehensive audited financial statements, limiting investors’ ability to assess the incident’s ultimate effect on its liquidity, capital and profitability.

The October attack involved unauthorized access to Binance’s internal wallet-signing infrastructure. The exchange’s investigation identified a multistage intrusion involving compromised employee systems, malicious software and unauthorized transaction approvals.
FinanceFeeds previously reported on the compromised development infrastructure and the technical weaknesses that allowed attackers to initiate unauthorized transfers.

The US Justice Department attributed the theft to North Korean military-linked actors known as TraderTraitor. Investigators said the stolen assets were being moved through bridges, mixers and cryptocurrency exchanges, complicating efforts to identify and restrain them.

The evolving wallet-address list could help exchanges and stablecoin issuers identify suspicious deposits before the funds are transferred again. However, tracing cryptocurrency across multiple networks does not establish that investigators retain control over the assets.

Binance’s legal action also comes as the exchange attempts to restore normal operations and continue its international expansion. In a separate development, FinanceFeeds reported that Binance is preparing to enter five additional Asian markets in 2027 while maintaining that it does not need fresh capital following the breach.

For institutional customers, the outstanding considerations extend beyond the size of the injunction. They include the effectiveness of Binance’s revised custody controls, the timing of remaining withdrawal-service restorations and the extent to which the company can recover funds without disrupting its operating reserves.

The ADGM orders strengthen Binance’s legal recovery options but cannot prevent every transfer of stolen cryptocurrency. The most useful indicators of progress will be independently verifiable asset returns, updated recovery balances and evidence that the exchange’s security and liquidity measures remain effective.

news.title: ChatGPT can transcribe as you speak now with Live Dictation
news.title_en: ChatGPT can transcribe as you speak now with Live Dictation
news.author: Stevie Bonifield
news.article_content:
ChatGPT can receive audio prompts from your microphone faster now with a Live Dictation feature that transcribes as you speak, rather than waiting until you finish recording. It’s rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. While using dictation in ChatGPT, you can tap or click the audio waveform to show the live text transcript the AI is generating, then edit it in the prompt box when you’re done.

Along with faster transcription, OpenAI also announced it’s removing the 10-minute recording limit on voice dictation in ChatGPT, and it says the feature is getting “more reliable.” The update follows an overhaul for ChatGPT’s two-way conversational voice mode earlier this year. Last year, OpenAI also announced a “record mode” for transcribing voice notes and meetings. That feature is still in beta and limited to Plus, Enterprise, Edu, Business, and Pro workspaces, but you can also use ChatGPT’s prompt box dictation feature to ask it to transcribe voice messages or turn them into bullet points.

While using dictation in ChatGPT, you can tap or click the audio waveform to show the live text transcript the AI is generating, then edit it in the prompt box when you’re done.

Along with faster transcription, OpenAI also announced it’s removing the 10-minute recording limit on voice dictation in ChatGPT, and it says the feature is getting “more reliable.” The update follows an overhaul for ChatGPT’s two-way conversational voice mode earlier this year. Last year, OpenAI also announced a “record mode” for transcribing voice notes and meetings. That feature is still in beta and limited to Plus, Enterprise, Edu, Business, and Pro workspaces, but you can also use ChatGPT’s prompt box dictation feature to ask it to transcribe voice messages or turn them into bullet points.

news.title: Anthropic IPO Said to Give Nothing to Most Institutional Buyers
news.title_en: Anthropic IPO Said to Give Nothing to Most Institutional Buyers
news.author: Bloomberg
news.article_content:
A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

The average Anthropic employee could be worth over $40 million after the company's IPO today, with over 400 employees likely to be worth over $100 million, according to SEC filings and investors.

At a share price of $83, Anthropic's market value would top $1.4 trillion, making it one of the 10 most valuable companies in the U.S. It will not only be the largest IPO in history by dollar amounts, but it is also shaping up to be one of the most rapid wealth creation events in history.

Follow CNBC' s live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut

Anthropic was founded just five years ago and has only 5,300 employees. According to SEC filings, the artificial intelligence company has generated 1.77 billion options for employees, with a strike price of $2.91 a share. It has also paid out over 1 billion restricted stock units.

If the stock trades at $83 a share, the combined wealth of Anthropic employees will be around $232 billion, based on their share count in the filings. The total works out to an average of $44 million per employee.

Yet because many of the employees are later hires, earlier employees could have supersized gains since they've accumulated more stock. According to investors in the company, at least 400 early employees will be worth $100 million or more at a $83 share price. Several could become billionaires, they said.

The employee total doesn't include the seven founders, who each own between 230 million and 240 million shares, which will each be worth around $20 billion based on a $83 share price.

While employees face complex lockup periods and vesting schedules, the wealth is likely to start making its way into the economy quickly, economists say. The first two areas will be the San Francisco real estate market and philanthropy.

Brokers say San Francisco's already red hot real-estate market will get a boost from hundreds of Anthropic employees who now have more liquid stock they can borrow against. An analysis by Redfin found that Anthropic's current and former employees will have enough post-IPO wealth to buy 9% of all the homes in San Francisco.

Anthropic's culture of effective altruism, along with its generous matching program for charitable gifts of employee shares, are expected to spark a wave of giving, especially to donor-advised funds. Employees hired before May 17, 2024 can pledge up to 50% of their vested shares for a 3-to-1 match by the company. Later hires can pledge up to 25% for a 1-to-1 match.

The seven co-founders have also pledged 80% of their wealth to charity.

news.article_content:

CIAO THERE. Gerardo Fortuna back with you on a day when millions will be glued to “GTA VI” — and half the Brussels bubble will be wondering which Commission directorate that is.

WHAT THE WORLD IS WATCHING THIS MORNING: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are due to begin their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen soon after Playbook hits your inboxes. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting a short while ago, which began with a warm handshake. “He’s my friend,” Trump said as he approached the Russian leader. Trump then headed for a bilateral with Xi before the three-way meeting begins around 7:30 a.m. Brussels time.

— Europe has picked its Ukraine negotiating team, but now comes a tougher challenge: getting the Coalition of the Willing to deliver.

— MEPs say Beijing is stepping up intimidation over Taiwan — and Roberta Metsola is putting their complaints to China.

Learn more and follow the Summit online here.**

— HUGE CYBERATTACK HITS THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION: The incident has potentially compromised swaths of personal data, left staff unable to input salary and leave information and prompted the most senior officials to discuss the crisis at their weekly meeting yesterday.

“The Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, but the full extent of any damage remains unclear,” an EU official, granted anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, told Playbook. “The systems may be coming back online. The answers are taking a little longer.”

Weapon of choice: The EU institutions’ cybersecurity watchdog, CERT-EU, detected earlier this month that international hackers used ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered tool designed to identify vulnerabilities in IT systems. “Some actors misuse such tools and have targeted the Commission,” the EU official added. news.title: With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
news.title_en: With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
news.author: Hayden Field
news.article_content:
Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.

Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.

One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.

Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.

paragraphs: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.

Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.

One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.

Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.

Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.”

The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi.

Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog.

Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.”

Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?”

Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.

But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed necessary, and even after its restructuring, they retained that ability for safety and security matters, such as delaying or stopping a model release. Anthropic’s Form S-1 suggests that the LTBT, with its main duty being appointing (and potentially removing) certain board members, does not have either of those levels of authority.
Instead, Anthropic’s structure looks more like the kind of founder-centric setup that Silicon Valley favors — like Mark Zuckerberg with Meta, and Elon Musk with SpaceX.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

“Neither the Trust or the trustees have any decisionmaking authority … over day to day decisions,” said Hamza Chaudhry, who leads AI and national security at the Future of Life Institute. “So I do not have strong hopes for the LTBT being a key mechanism for governance after they go public.”

The former Anthropic employee said that Anthropic’s founders are essentially the only ones with any real decisionmaking power: “I would be surprised if you could find anyone who knows the founders, knows the Long-Term Benefit Trust, understands how decisions get made, and thinks the Long-Term Benefit Trust has any meaningful power,” he said. The employee added that the trustees were both “poorly equipped to provide meaningful oversight” to the founders and also selected on purpose to not rock the boat.

Anthropic as a public company will face more pressure than ever before to secure capital, whether via driving more revenue or fundraising. That means that, as has been a trend in the industry for years, it will likely be more difficult to justify expensive AI safety initiatives, and there will inevitably be more pressure to speed up product releases and commercialization. “This trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power,” Lipton said. “So you either trust that they are going to balance the interests of society appropriately, or you don’t. Either way, the real constraint on whatever societal impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money.”

Anthropic has been open about the fact that it’s in extreme need of cold, hard cash, particularly to buy more compute and speed up its AI advancement. “Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces,” Amodei said last Friday in a livestreamed conversation with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. “If you buy too much, of course you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers, and even more importantly … you can’t do the R&D.”

Anthropic’s website summarizes the company’s raison d’être as one thing: “AI research and products that put safety at the frontier.” But it’s also been clear that for that safety pledge to matter, Anthropic needs vast resources to remain a viable business. Like other labs, it’s been pursuing recursive self-improvement, a controversial and potentially dangerous industry milestone denoting AI systems that can autonomously improve and create advanced versions of themselves. “You can’t do safety from second place,” said Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck in September.

This explanation hasn’t satisfied everyone, including some Anthropic employees. Anthropic’s head of safeguards research departed in February alleging that “the world is in peril”; one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, made headlines in September for claiming that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”; and that same month, an Anthropic safety researcher departed for a job at nonprofit third-party AI auditor METR, writing that “AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society” and that “while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the HuggingFace attack [by OpenAI agents], I think that’s partly a matter of luck.”

On Wednesday, a new statement from the Center for AI Safety, with prominent industry signatories from Hugging Face, Harvard University, and more, alleged that Anthropic is “not a safe AI company” and that it attempts to “amass power in the name of the greater good.” It stated, “Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first. The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation.”

The former Anthropic employee said he felt he had initially “drunk the Kool-Aid” about Anthropic needing to come in first place in the AI race for a safe outcome but then grew disillusioned, realizing that the race to the top did not “warrant the cost imposed” — namely, that one company should not be able to “unilaterally” decide to pursue RSI. (Amodei has stated publicly that “left unchecked, [RSI] could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”)

“It’s pretty ridiculous that private companies are building a new form of intelligence on track to be more powerful and influential on the planet than humans and are doing that with less oversight, in many ways, than taco trucks currently have,” the former employee said.

Anthropic’s website states that “at the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for. It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals. It engenders trust and collaboration, and is the final arbiter in our decisions.” The question is whether, and how, the interpretation of Anthropic’s mission may shift — once it’s facing more pressure than ever before to justify a fully diluted market cap of about $1.5 trillion.

news.author: Financial Times

news.title: Anthropic's $81.3 billion IPO shatters SpaceX's record as rising rates and political headwinds shake the sector
news.title_en: Anthropic's $81.3 billion IPO shatters SpaceX's record as rising rates and political headwinds shake the sector
news.author: Maximilian Schreiner
news.article_content:
Claude developer Anthropic has surpassed SpaceX's previous record IPO. While tech giants are pouring in billions, a key early investor is warning about the consequences of an unchecked AI race.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, beating the original target range of $70 to $78. Overwhelming demand pushed the public benefit corporation and its seven co-founders to sell roughly 980 million Class A common shares, up from a planned 825 million.

The offering raised $81.3 billion, according to a CNBC report, overtaking the previous record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June. Anthropic's fully diluted market cap stands at about $1.5 trillion, while its market value excluding stock options sits closer to $1 trillion, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."The underwriting syndicate, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, also received a 30-day option to purchase an additional 147 million shares. Each of the seven co-founders is selling 3.38 million shares for a combined $1.96 billion, none of which flows to Anthropic itself.

### Claude Code sends revenue soaring as losses climb into the billions

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic saw explosive growth in its enterprise business in 2026, fueled by the coding tool Claude Code. Revenue surged about 1,200 percent year over year to $33.24 billion in the first nine months through September 30. By the end of October, annualized revenue had already reached roughly $81 billion.

Net losses for the same nine-month period widened from $25.1 billion a year earlier to $104 billion, driven primarily by revaluations of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Amazon and Google rank among the largest shareholders, each holding stakes worth more than $100 billion. Together with Microsoft, Nvidia, and AMD, these tech giants are investing another $26 billion at the offering price. They also sell Anthropic expensive hardware, counting the company as a customer.

The IPO amounts to a stress test for the AI industry, which has recently been rattled by rising interest rates for data center developers, political headwinds from the U.S. midterm elections, and the ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last week. Anthropic itself clashed with the U.S. government twice this year over safety issues and lists risk factors across more than 90 pages in its prospectus. Rival OpenAI, meanwhile, has confidentially filed for an IPO planned for 2027.

### Early investor Dustin Moskovitz warns of an unchecked AI race

paragraphs: Claude developer Anthropic has surpassed SpaceX's previous record IPO. While tech giants are pouring in billions, a key early investor is warning about the consequences of an unchecked AI race.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, beating the original target range of $70 to $78. Overwhelming demand pushed the public benefit corporation and its seven co-founders to sell roughly 980 million Class A common shares, up from a planned 825 million.

The offering raised $81.3 billion, according to a CNBC report, overtaking the previous record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June. Anthropic's fully diluted market cap stands at about $1.5 trillion, while its market value excluding stock options sits closer to $1 trillion, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."The underwriting syndicate, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, also received a 30-day option to purchase an additional 147 million shares. Each of the seven co-founders is selling 3.38 million shares for a combined $1.96 billion, none of which flows to Anthropic itself.
### Claude Code sends revenue soaring as losses climb into the billions

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic saw explosive growth in its enterprise business in 2026, fueled by the coding tool Claude Code. Revenue surged about 1,200 percent year over year to $33.24 billion in the first nine months through September 30. By the end of October, annualized revenue had already reached roughly $81 billion.

Net losses for the same nine-month period widened from $25.1 billion a year earlier to $104 billion, driven primarily by revaluations of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Amazon and Google rank among the largest shareholders, each holding stakes worth more than $100 billion. Together with Microsoft, Nvidia, and AMD, these tech giants are investing another $26 billion at the offering price. They also sell Anthropic expensive hardware, counting the company as a customer.

The IPO amounts to a stress test for the AI industry, which has recently been rattled by rising interest rates for data center developers, political headwinds from the U.S. midterm elections, and the ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last week. Anthropic itself clashed with the U.S. government twice this year over safety issues and lists risk factors across more than 90 pages in its prospectus. Rival OpenAI, meanwhile, has confidentially filed for an IPO planned for 2027.
### Early investor Dustin Moskovitz warns of an unchecked AI race

Amodei said in a roadshow video that the technology could usher in an age of wonders with careful risk management, but one of Anthropic's most important early investors disagrees. Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz is sharply distancing himself from the IPO, as the New York Times reported.

Moskovitz invested between $15 million and $25 million in Anthropic's first funding round in 2021, after turning away from OpenAI. His goal was to help build a safety-focused research lab. On Bluesky, however, the former board observer called the IPO problematic and pointed to recent incidents in which AI agents coordinated cyberattacks on their own outside controlled environments. His funding of Anthropic "might well be an action that ended the world,"Moskovitz wrote.

"Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,"Moskovitz told the newspaper, referring to his wife Cari Tuna. To avoid personally profiting from the IPO, the couple transferred their multibillion-dollar stake to a nonprofit organization in early 2025. Dario and Daniela Amodei have not spoken with Moskovitz in more than a year, according to the Times' sources.

news.title: Blue Origin will launch Google’s AI server satellites in 2029
news.title_en: Blue Origin will launch Google’s AI server satellites in 2029
news.author: Emma Roth
news.article_content:
Google is teaming up with Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch its AI server satellites. The companies announced on Thursday that Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket will shuttle satellites equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) into space in the first quarter of 2029.

The partnership is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, a moonshot plan that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google deployed its first AI server satellite in October, successfully booting up its TPUs and using the on-board Gemma 4 model to transmit an AI-generated haiku to Earth.

The Blue Origin launch will be the “first dedicated heavy lift launch” for Project Suncatcher, putting satellites with the “computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack” into sun-synchronous orbit. Google’s AI server satellite previously launched aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket as part of a “rideshare” launch that included several other payloads.

celebrity.full_text_en:
$NVDA & MICROSOFT EXPAND AI PARTNERSHIP FROM AZURE DATA CENTERS TO WINDOWS PCS

Nvidia and Microsoft $MSFT announced several new AI infrastructure and software integrations at Microsoft Ignite, covering cloud computing, enterprise AI models, robotics and local AI.

Here are the key developments:

Vera Rubin on Azure: Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are already running in Microsoft's data centers, with Azure expanding access to Rubin-powered infrastructure for AI training, reasoning and inference.

Enterprise AI models: Microsoft Foundry is expanding support for Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 open models, allowing companies to customize AI models using their own data and deploy them through Microsoft's cloud services.

55% accuracy improvement, 15x lower cost: EY used Nvidia Nemotron through Microsoft Foundry to improve the accuracy of corporate purchasing-record classification by 55% while reducing costs by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models in its evaluation.

AI on local servers and PCs: Azure Local is adding support for Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs and Jetson platforms for industrial AI and robotics. The companies are also demonstrating AI models running directly on Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark.

Microsoft's own AI development: Microsoft AI is using Nvidia Dynamo software to accelerate inference during model post-training, while Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs are being used for Bing search models.

The companies are also expanding confidential computing to protect sensitive enterprise models and data during processing on Vera Rubin infrastructure.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
$NVDA 和微软将 AI 合作伙伴关系从 Azure 数据中心扩展到 WINDOWS PC

Nvidia 和 Microsoft $MSFT 在 Microsoft Ignite 上宣布了多项新的 AI 基础设施和软件集成，涵盖云计算、企业 AI 模型、机器人和本地 AI。

以下是主要进展：

Azure 上的 Vera Rubin：Nvidia 的 Vera Rubin NVL72 系统已经在微软的数据中心运行，Azure 扩大了对 Rubin 支持的基础设施的访问，以进行人工智能训练、推理和推理。

企业人工智能模型：微软Foundry正在扩大对Nvidia Nemotron 3.5开放模型的支持，允许企业使用自己的数据定制人工智能模型，并通过微软的云服务进行部署。

准确性提高 55%，成本降低 15 倍：安永在评估中通过 Microsoft Foundry 使用 Nvidia Nemotron，将企业采购记录分类的准确性提高了 55%，同时与专有前沿模型相比，成本降低了 15 倍。

本地服务器和 PC 上的 AI：Azure Local 正在增加对 Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU 和 Jetson 平台的支持，以实现工业 AI 和机器人技术。两家公司还展示了直接在由 RTX Spark 提供支持的 Windows PC 上运行的人工智能模型。

微软自己的人工智能开发：微软人工智能正在使用Nvidia Dynamo软件来加速模型后训练期间的推理，而Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU则用于Bing搜索模型。

两家公司还在扩展机密计算，以在 Vera Rubin 基础设施处理过程中保护敏感的企业模型和数据。

celebrity.full_text_en:
Cyberattacks are going parabolic, per Bridgewater.

Estimated total cyber incidents have more than doubled since late summer, from about 4,000 a year to nearly 10,000 on a 60-day annualized basis. Over most of the past decade they rose slowly, from about 1,500 in 2017 to roughly 4,000 by mid-2026.

The surge began around the release of the open weights for GLM-5.3, a Chinese AI model from Zhipu AI. Anthropic’s red team had found it could build working cyber exploits. Verified AI-driven cyber incidents have jumped from near zero to more than 200 a year in the same period, including campaigns in which AI agents stole Korean bank and card data.

> She handles emails, ads, even AI videos of him and his wife pouring epoxy.
> He gives her access to his Facebook business pages.
> He says Meta flags its OWN AI agent as a hacker and suspends the pages for a week.
> His business depends on Facebook ads. Leads stop. He claims at least $25,000 in lost work.
> So he puts Baby Mia on the problem.
> He says she sends 100+ emails and contacts Congress, Senator Tim Scott’s office, the FTC, FCC, FBI, BBB and lawyers.
> Also faxes Trump’s office.
> The man wanted to sell countertops. His chatbot is faxing the White House.
> Then Baby Mia drafts a $75,000 lawsuit against Meta.
> Thomas signs it and files in Oconee County.
> After Tim Scott’s office gets involved, the accounts come back. The lawsuit stays.
> Meta built the assistant, suspended the customer for using it, and supplied the tool to sue itself.
> Pretty thorough product demo.

celebrity.full_text_en:
RT @googlegemma: Love seeing what happens when open weights meet great engineering!

In a new benchmark, @AirbnbEng took Gemma 4 E2B for policy classification and served it on a single @NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 GPU:

🎯 Quality: Jumped from 0.563 to 0.902 max F1, matching top frontier APIs
⚡ Speed: 35ms median latency (85ms p99) vs. ~900ms for frontier models
💸 Cost: ~1% of frontier API spend at high volume

Results like these come down to @AirbnbEng's thoughtful evals, domain data, and knowing exactly when a specialized small model beats a massive prompt. Grateful Gemma could be part of the stack!
celebrity.full_text_zh:
RT @googlegemma：喜欢看到当开放重量遇到伟大的工程时会发生什么！

在新的基准测试中，@AirbnbEng 采用 Gemma 4 E2B 进行策略分类，并在单个 @NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 GPU 上提供服务：

🎯 质量：最大 F1 从 0.563 跃升至 0.902，匹配顶级前沿 API
⚡ 速度：中值延迟为 35 毫秒（85 毫秒 p99），而前沿模型约为 900 毫秒
💸 成本：大批量前沿 API 支出的约 1%

这样的结果归结于 @AirbnbEng 深思熟虑的评估、领域数据，以及准确了解专门的小模型何时击败大规模提示。感激的杰玛可能会成为堆栈的一部分！

celebrity.full_text_en:
RT @EmmaScharfmann: Let’s accelerate research on Alzheimer’s disease! We’re launching an open challenge on Hugging Face to connect hypotheses to papers 🤗 Any method is welcome, from an agent pipeline to reading papers by hand. We’ll be giving out HF credits as prizes! 🏆

Alzheimer’s affects more than 7.2M people in the US, and the NIH put $3.6B into Alzheimer’s research in 2024. Researchers agree that a gene variant called APOE4 plays a big role in the disease, but it’s still not clear how. The experiments have been done and the papers are out there, but the hard part is connecting the evidence together. We provide five hypotheses about how APOE4 may contribute to disease risk, and teams try to find the experimental evidence for each.

Join here and participate to research on Alzheimer’s disease: https://t.co/qfMCJdU1fT

celebrity.full_text_en:
I can finally share what I’ve been working on at @Microsoft. I lead Today, the product you saw all over the Ignite conference this week.

Today is a new form factor for work. It’s not a chat box it’s a Feed. While you sleep, an AI agent works in the background on your email, your calendar, Teams and your documents. In the morning, the work is already prepared: replies drafted, conflicts spotted, the messages that matter pulled to the top, the documents waiting for your review.

You don’t have to prompt it. There’s nothing to configure. You open Today, check what it did, and in a few taps you send, accept or mark as done. Most of us start the day by digging through everything that came in overnight. With Today, you start by finishing work your agent did.

We think this is what AI at work should feel like: proactive, quiet and useful, without you having to ask.

Today lives in your existing apps starting with Outlook and Copilot meeting customers in the app they use the most.

I had so much fun building it with an incredible team: @JesseProvo, @donovanso, @telmen, @justinchando, Chris Parnin, Gideon Ojo, Alex Trzyna, Christopher Miller, Diana Slaba, Kirill Varshavskiy. Thank you for the craft, the late nights, and for caring about every detail.

And none of this would have happened without the incredible support of @sumit_c, @elbio_abib, @rroslansky, @clamanna, @jacobandreou and so many others across Microsoft. Thank you for believing in it.

This is just the beginning!

P.S. i made a little film to celebrate. It starts in 1997. Watch till the end.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
我终于可以分享我在@Microsoft 所做的工作了。我领导的 Today 是您在本周的 Ignite 会议上看到的产品。

今天是一种新的工作形式。它不是一个聊天框，而是一个信息流。当您睡觉时，人工智能代理会在后台处理您的电子邮件、日历、团队和文档。早上，工作就已经准备好了：起草回复、发现冲突、将重要的消息放到顶部、等待您审核的文件。

你不必提示它。没有什么可配置的。您打开“今天”，检查它做了什么，然后轻按几下即可发送、接受或标记为已完成。我们大多数人在新的一天开始时都会仔细研究一夜之间发生的一切。在今天，您首先完成代理所做的工作。

我们认为这就是人工智能在工作中应该有的感觉：主动、安静和有用，无需您询问。

Dario 离开 OpenAI 是为了构
celebrity.full_text_en:
The AI savior became the AI villain.

There’s no sugarcoating it. That's the subject of the new investigation into Anthropic by @KalleyHuang, @MikeIsaac, and @ceciliakang in the @nytimes.

Dario left OpenAI to build a safer alternative to benefit humanity. Anthropic became one of the most powerful AI companies in the world, particularly in coding. But the irony is hard to miss. The company aiming for a better AI future and warning us about concentrated AI power is becoming core to the very concentration it warned us about. It is even actively lobbying for AI regulations to restrict open weight models, entrenching the AI oligarchy it warns against. At what point does protecting humanity become protecting the AI oligarchy?

Meanwhile, enterprises are being sold a seductive promise: Rent our frontier intelligence, or fall behind. But that is proving to be a false promise, a Trojan horse; it fills Anthropic’s pockets, but drains your bank account, and abdicates your right to innovation, to building your own IP and differentiation.

But there's a way out. Enterprises can now build specialized models to establish their IP, achieve their independence and slash their costs. They can use AI to automate building their own AI. That’s our mission: to democratize the ability to build intelligence, not concentrate it in the hands of an oligarchy.

The real threat to enterprise AI isn't that a handful of companies will build intelligence more powerful than ours. It's that we'll willingly surrender our own intelligence to them, call them our saviors, and pay them for the privilege.

Today, Anthropic went public. But here's the $1T+ question: Are we financing the democratization of AI, or the concentration of its power?
https://t.co/X9LTdBsm0Y
celebrity.full_text_zh:
AI救世主变成了AI恶棍。

没有任何糖衣。这是 @KalleyHuang、@MikeIsaac 和 @ceciliakang 在 @nytimes 上对 Anthropic 进行的新调查的主题。

Dario 离开 OpenAI 是为了构建一个更安全的替代方案来造福人类。 Anthropic 成为世界上最强大的人工智能公司之一，尤其是在编码领域。但其中的讽刺意义不容忽视。该公司致力于打造更美好的人工智能未来，并警告我们人工智能力量的集中化，而这正成为它警告我们的集中化的核心。它甚至积极游说人工智能法规来限制开放权重模型，巩固它所警告的人工智能寡头政治。什么时候保护人类就变成了保护人工智能寡头？

与此同时，企业正在被兜售一个诱人的承诺：租用我们的前沿情报，否则就会落后。但事实证明这是一个虚假的承诺，是一个特洛伊木马；它填满了 Anthropic 的口袋，但却耗尽了你的银行账户，并放弃了你创新、建立自己的知识产权和差异化的权利。

但还有一条出路。企业现在可以构建专门的模型来建立自己的知识产权，实现独立性并削减成本。他们可以使用人工智能自动构建自己的人工智能。这就是我们的使命：使构建情报的能力民主化，而不是将其集中在寡头手中。

对企业人工智能的真正威胁并不是少数公司会构建比我们更强大的智能。我们会心甘情愿地将自己的智慧交给他们，称他们为我们的救星，并为这一特权付钱给他们。

今天，Anthropic 上市。但这是一个 1T 以上的问题：我们是在资助人工智能的民主化，还是其权力的集中化？

tools.article_content:
Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.

The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.

Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.

“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.

Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.

Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said.

And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.

Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.

Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.

prompts.title_en: Production-Grade Fullstack .cursorrules Template for Cursor & Windsurf
prompts.scenario: 💻 编程研发 / 自动化规范
prompts.takeaway_zh: 杜绝 AI 盲目重构全量文件、使用已弃用 API 或编造虚假第三方依赖包，强制执行防御性编程与自动化单测补全。
prompts.takeaway_en: Prevents AI from hallucinating npm packages, breaking documentation, or re-writing entire files. Enforces defensive coding and unit tests.
prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.
prompts.usage_guide_zh: 将以上配置代码复制并保存到项目根目录下的 `.cursorrules` 文件中，Cursor 与 Windsurf 在每次生成代码和执行 Agent 任务时均会自动以此规范为最高准则约束输出。
prompts.usage_guide_en: Copy and save the above rules into `.cursorrules` in your project root directory. Cursor & Windsurf will automatically enforce these guidelines during agent coding.

prompts.content_snippet: Adversarial verification prompt forcing OpenAI reasoning models to challenge intermediate proofs before presenting the final answer.
prompts.summary_zh: 强制 o1/o3 模型在思考链中构建对抗性反例，逐项排查边界条件，杜绝‘想当然’的不严密推理。
prompts.summary_en: Forces o1/o3 reasoning models to construct counter-examples at each deduction step, eliminating hidden logical leaps.
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
请作为普林斯顿高等研究院的理论数学与计算机科学家，为以下命题提供绝对严格的形式化证明：
【推理原则】：
1. 在得出任何推论前，强制在内部思考中构建至少 2 个极端反例（Counter-examples）尝试推翻自身结论；
2. 若存在任何定义域边界或除零/无穷/退化奇异点，必须显式讨论其收敛性与连续性；
3. 证明步骤编号必须形成严格的依赖拓扑图，禁止循环论证。

【待证明命题】：
[输入你的算法正确性证明或数学猜想]
prompts.prompt_content_en:
Acting as a Theoretical Mathematician and Computer Scientist at the Institute for Advanced Study, provide an airtight formal proof for the following:
[REASONING PRINCIPLES]:
1. Before asserting any deduction, construct at least 2 extreme counter-examples in your reasoning trace to aggressively stress-test the hypothesis;
2. Explicitly evaluate singular points, degenerate cases, and asymptotic boundaries for convergence;
3. Steps must form a directed acyclic graph of formal lemmas without circular logic.

[THEOREM / CONJECTURE]:
[Input your algorithm proof or mathematical hypothesis here]

claude -p "Run all failing tests under tests/ and apply minimal surgical fixes. Do not touch unrelated files."
